cards.question: Why is methaemoglobin clinically dangerous?
cards.answer: In methaemoglobin the haem iron is oxidised from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and cannot bind oxygen, while remaining haems bind O₂ more tightly (left-shifted curve) — so tissue delivery falls. Levels >15% cause cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen; >50% cause coma; >70% are fatal. Treat with IV methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg, which regenerates Fe²⁺ via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase.

cards.question: How does a fuel cell oxygen analyser work?
cards.answer: In a lead/gold galvanic (fuel) oxygen cell, oxygen is reduced at the gold cathode (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻), while lead is oxidised at the anode (Pb + 2OH⁻ → PbO + H₂O + 2e⁻). The resulting current is proportional to O₂ partial pressure. It is self-powered, accurate to ±3%, and lasts typically 1–2 years because the anode is consumed.

cards.question: Which inhaled anaesthetics are degraded by CO₂ absorbents?
cards.answer: Sevoflurane reacts with strong bases (KOH, NaOH) in soda-lime to form Compound A, a vinyl ether with renal toxicity in rats. Desflurane, enflurane and isoflurane (in descending order of risk; sevoflurane produces little) react with desiccated CO₂ absorbent to generate carbon monoxide. Both risks are mitigated by using KOH/NaOH-free absorbents (e.g. Amsorb Plus) and avoiding desiccated absorbent.
